 Flood-ready on the Oregon Coast How to prepare for a flood and manage the aftermath

 Español

 EM 9927 
 | November 2026 
 | 
 Download PDF 
 Flooding in Pacific City, Oregon, in December 2014. Rain, tides and storm surges can combine to create flooding anywhere along the Oregon Coast.
 Credit: J.X. Bauer
 Contents
 Causes of coastal floods 
 How to prepare 
 After a flood 
 Resources 
 Acknowledgments 
 Floods can cause landslides and power outages, damage buildings and roads, and cause septic systems and wastewater treatment plants to overflow. Floods also may isolate people or communities.
 Learn what you can do to prepare before flooding hits, and what to do during a flood or flood warning. This guide also includes information on what to do after a flood, and lists resources you can call on for help.
 Section anchor "causes-coastal-floods" 
 Causes of coastal floods
 Severe coastal floods typically occur when two or more of these factors coincide.
 High tides
 The gravitational pull of the moon and sun cause the ocean to rise and fall. Oregon has two unequal high tides and low tides daily. King tides, extremely high tides that occur in winter, can cause flooding.
 Large waves
 Strong offshore winds can create tall, powerful waves. Larger winds can push more water toward shore.
 Storm surges
 Strong winds push water toward shore. When winds combine with low atmospheric pressure, water levels rise.
 Water level anomalies
 Warmer than typical water and anomalous storm conditions can also raise water levels, particularly during an El Niño.
 Sea level rise
 Sea levels rise because a warming climate expands the oceans and melts glaciers and ice sheets.
 Heavy rain
 When substantial rain falls within a short period, water often cannot drain rapidly. Runoff occurs when the land cannot absorb more water. Rivers or streams may overflow.
 Tsunamis
 A tsunami is a series of waves caused by a large undersea earthquake, landslide or volcanic activity. Distant tsunamis may be caused by earthquakes across the ocean. These waves reach Oregon a few hours after the quake. Local tsunamis may be caused by nearby offshore earthquakes. These waves come ashore within 10 to 20 minutes of the earthquake and can be devastating.
 Section anchor "how-to-prepare" 
 How to prepare
 Check weather forecasts and tsunami and flood maps.
 Sign up for local emergency alerts at oralert.gov. 
 Enable wireless emergency alerts on your mobile device.
 Know your local emergency utility numbers.
 Purchase a transistor or emergency weather radio.
 Learn your hazard warning signals, evacuation routes and shelter locations.
 Make copies of important documents and receipts for valuables. Store them electronically and in waterproof containers.
 Pack an emergency kit or a “go bag.”
 Stay up to date on tetanus shots. Most adults should receive a tetanus booster every 10 years.
 Keep a fire extinguisher handy in your residence and and your vehicle.
 Obtain a generator, or know which neighbors have generators.
 Create a family evacuation and communication plan.
 Store three to five days’ worth of bottled water and food for each household member. Estimate 1 gallon of water per person per day.
 Fix leaks, seal cracks and clear gutters and drains at your residence.
 Place sandbags around your residence and move your belongings to a higher elevation if you expect flooding.
 If your residence is in a flood zone
 Elevate electrical systems.
 Anchor fuel tanks.
 Install sump pumps and backflow valves.
 Purchase flood or renter’s insurance.
 Section anchor "during-flood" 
 During a flood or flood warning
 Tune in to radio or television stations for weather and water level updates.
 Follow state or county emergency instructions.
 Fill tubs, sinks and bottles with clean water.
 Get your home, vehicle, family and pets ready to evacuate.
 Turn off gas, power and water if necessary or before evacuating.
 Do not walk or drive through floodwaters.
 Do not approach downed power lines.
 Call 911 in case of emergencies.
 Section anchor "after-flood" 
 After a flood
 Check for damage to electrical, gas, sewage and water lines.
 Do not try to start flooded vehicles or use wet electrical appliances.
 Do not use floodwater for food preparation.
 Wear protective gear, such as rubber boots and gloves, during cleanup.
 Use fans, air conditioning and dehumidifiers to dry out your home.
 Call professionals for assistance if possible.
 Discard flood-contaminated food; save undamaged canned goods.
 Shovel out mud, hose down exterior surfaces and clean walls and floors.
 Take photographs and videos of damage to your home and belongings.
 Keep samples of ruined items.
 Save repair receipts from contractors or purchases of supplies.
 Report damage to your insurer.
 Remove mold promptly. Flood insurance often doesn’t cover mold removal.
 Reach out to local agencies if you need support.
 Take care of your mental health.
